Testing a serverless, event-driven flow (SQS + DLQ + DynamoDB) locally for $0 with LocalStack and Java 21 Post link: AWS Study Group
Author(s): Ngô Thị Kim Ngân · Published: November 27, 2026
Summary The post shows how to test an asynchronous flow (event → SQS → Java 21 Lambda → DynamoDB / SSM Parameter Store, with a DLQ) on a local machine with LocalStack before deploying with AWS SAM. The aim is to fix small bugs locally instead of on AWS, which is faster and avoids unexpected charges.
Key points In the AWS SDK for Java v2, call endpointOverride with http://localhost:4566 only in local mode. In the cloud, use the default endpoint. Test both paths: a valid payload must be written to DynamoDB and deleted from the main queue; a failing payload must land in the DLQ after the configured number of retries. Deploy with SAM only after the logic and configuration work locally.

title: Overview
content:
The problem Elderly people in Vietnam receive a steady stream of scam messages: fake traffic fines, fake bank or public-service notices, “your child is in hospital, transfer money now”, phishing links. Many of them do not have someone nearby to ask at the moment the message arrives, and by the time they ask, the money is gone.
The solution Ask First puts a “third person” between the message and the money. The user forwards the suspicious text, link or screenshot to a Telegram bot. The bot:
Replies with “⏳” right away, so the user knows it is working. Reads the content (OCR for screenshots), masks personal numbers, runs fixed rules and a small knowledge base of known scam scenarios, and only then asks an LLM to judge. Edits the “⏳” message into a short answer in plain Vietnamese: a risk level, the scam pattern it matches, why, and what to do now. If the risk is high and the user has linked a relative (double opt-in), sends that relative an alert. The bot does not store the original message: only the verdict, signal codes and hashes, with a TTL.
Architecture The diagram follows one check from start to end. The numbers below match the numbered arrows.
Step What happens 1–2 The elderly user sends a message. Telegram POSTs the update to the webhook Lambda Function URL with the header X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token. The function rejects any request without the right secret (HTTP 401). 3 webhook de-duplicates the update_id, checks that the user has given consent, and appends the message to a per-chat buffer (BUFFER#) in DynamoDB, so several messages sent in a row are checked together. 4 webhook sends “⏳” to the user, puts a job on the SQS jobs queue with a 3-second delay, and returns HTTP 200 to Telegram in under a second. 5–6 The worker Lambda (Java) polls the queue (maximum concurrency 5), reads the buffer and the kill-switch flags (CONFIG#global/FLAGS), then invokes the ai Lambda synchronously with op=analyze. Only metadata and Telegram file_ids are sent, never image bytes. 7 ai downloads the image from Telegram straight into memory, using the bot token it reads from SSM Parameter Store. 8 On a cold start, ai lazily downloads model weights (OCR, embedder) and the knowledge-base index from S3 into /tmp and checks their SHA-256. 9 ai reads and writes only cache items (CACHE#, URL#) in DynamoDB. The same content checked twice in 24 hours is answered from cache. 10–12 The pipeline runs Normalize → Extract (OCR) → Mask PII → Signals (rules + URL intel) → Retrieve (RAG) → Guard → Judge → Fuse → Respond. Bedrock Guardrails checks for prompt attacks, then Bedrock (Qwen3 32B in Sydney, escalating to gpt-oss-120b when unsure) judges the masked text. If the rules are already certain, the LLM is skipped. 13–15 worker edits the “⏳” message into the result. If the verdict is dangerous and a relative is linked, it sends the relative an alert with an “I have contacted them” button. 16–17 worker stores a CHECK# record (metadata only, TTL 30 days) and may schedule a 15-minute follow-up job on SQS. A job that fails 5 times moves to the DLQ; a small worker-dlq Lambda tells the user the bot is busy, and a CloudWatch alarm fires. The diagram shows the team’s running dev stack (checked on 25/11/2026): 4 Lambda functions, Bedrock in a separate account that ai assumes a role into, and the DLQ alarm emailing through SNS. When you deploy it yourself with this workshop: SnapStart is off by default (WorkerSnapStart=None), VietOCR is optional, the SNS topic for the alarm is optional (AlarmTopicArn, section 5.7.5), Bedrock is called in your own account unless you set BEDROCK_ROLE_ARN, and GitHub Actions only builds and pushes the ai image through OIDC; sam deploy is run by hand.
Services used and why Service Role in Ask First Why this choice AWS Lambda webhook, worker, worker-dlq (Java 21 zip) and ai (Python container image) Traffic is small and bursty, so pay per request. A Function URL gives an HTTPS endpoint without API Gateway. A container image lets ai ship ML libraries that exceed the 250 MB zip limit. Amazon SQS + DLQ Queue between webhook and worker webhook can answer Telegram immediately; retries (max 5) and a DLQ come for free; DelaySeconds implements the 3-second debounce and the 15-minute follow-up without a scheduler. Amazon DynamoDB Single table askfirst-<stage>: users, consent, buffers, checks, cache, flags On-demand billing, TTL deletes data automatically (data minimisation), conditional writes for idempotency, PITR enabled. Amazon S3 Model weights, knowledge-base index, donated samples (donated/, expires after 30 days) Cheap storage; models can change without rebuilding the image. Block Public Access and SSE are on. Amazon Bedrock LLM judge (Qwen3 32B, backup gpt-oss-120b) in ap-southeast-2 Serverless, pay per token, no GPU to run. Open-weight models were available in Sydney but not in Singapore when the team chose them. Bedrock Guardrails Detects prompt attacks in the input The message content is untrusted by nature. Amazon ECR Stores the ai image (askfirst-ai, keeps the 5 newest images) Required for Lambda container images. SSM Parameter Store Bot token and webhook secret (SecureString), plus stack config Secrets stay out of code and out of Lambda configuration; the standard tier has no extra cost. Amazon CloudWatch Logs of every function, alarm askfirst-<stage>-jobs-dlq-not-empty Built in, no extra agent. AWS SAM / CloudFormation Whole stack as code (infra/template.yaml) One command builds and deploys; the same template creates dev or prod. IAM + GitHub OIDC Least-privilege roles; GitHub Actions pushes the image without long-lived keys No access keys stored in GitHub. Services deliberately not used: API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, OpenSearch, VPC/NAT Gateway (a NAT Gateway alone costs about 32 USD/month), and self-hosted GPUs on EC2/SageMaker (source: docs/system-architecture.md §3.2 in the project repository).
Mapping to the AWS Well-Architected pillars Pillar How Ask First addresses it Operational excellence Infrastructure as code with SAM; CI on GitHub Actions (Maven verify, pytest, contract tests between Java and Python); JSON logs share a trace_id across worker and ai; DLQ alarm. Security Function URL accepts only requests with the Telegram secret header; secrets in SSM SecureString, decryptable only through SSM (kms:ViaService); least-privilege IAM (for example ai may only touch DynamoDB keys starting with CACHE# or URL#, and only some S3 prefixes); S3 Block Public Access and encryption; personal numbers are masked before any text leaves for Bedrock; OIDC instead of access keys in CI. Reliability SQS retries with ReportBatchItemFailures, DLQ after 5 failures, update_id de-duplication, degraded “rules only” mode when the LLM fails, DynamoDB PITR. Performance efficiency Three functions sized for their job (fast webhook, worker up to 120 s, ai with 3008 MB and 90 s); small CPU models loaded lazily and cached in memory; verdict cache for repeated content. Cost optimization Pure pay-per-use, no VPC/NAT, on-demand DynamoDB, low-cost open-weight models, the LLM is skipped when rules are certain. Measured Bedrock cost was about 0.00076 USD per text check (source: docs/results/lambda-p95.md, 100 checks on 2026-11-24). Sustainability No idle servers: every component scales to zero when nobody sends messages.

title: Blog 2
content:
Lambda + EventBridge: using event-driven architecture to refresh data every day Post link: AWS Study Group
Author(s): Võ Đức Trí · Published: November 27, 2026
Summary The post builds a static page that refreshes fuel prices, gold prices, esports scores and the weather on its own, instead of opening several tabs every morning. EventBridge Scheduler invokes a collector Lambda at a separate rate for each source; the collector writes JSON to S3; the S3 event goes through EventBridge to a renderer Lambda that rebuilds index.html and invalidates CloudFront. The parts never call each other directly, so one failing source does not break the page.
Key points One shared collector; each schedule sends its own source name as the payload. Scheduler supports time zones, a retry policy and a DLQ. The collector normalizes data into data/<source>.json. A failing source raises an error and does not overwrite the old file, so the page keeps the last good data. The EventBridge rule must filter on the data/ prefix. Otherwise the index.html written by the renderer triggers the renderer again, forever. S3 delivers events at least once, so the renderer must be idempotent: it always rebuilds the whole page from current data and overwrites it. Each section shows its updatedAt so readers can tell which numbers are stale.

title: Prerequisites
content:
Prepare everything on this page before you start 5.3. Commands are written for macOS/Linux (or Git Bash on Windows). PowerShell versions of the SSM commands are in infra/README.md of the project repository.
1. AWS account and Regions You need an AWS account where you can create IAM roles. Use a sandbox or dev account, not production.
Region Used for ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) Everything you deploy: Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB, S3, SSM, ECR, CloudWatch. Fixed in infra/samconfig.toml and .github/workflows/ai-image.yml. ap-southeast-2 (Sydney) Amazon Bedrock models and the Guardrail only (bedrock_region in ai/config/models.yaml). Nothing is deployed there by SAM. Create an AWS Budgets cost budget before you start. The team used alerts at 10, 25 and 50 USD (Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create budget).
2. Amazon Bedrock models in ap-southeast-2 The ai function calls two models in Sydney:
Purpose Model ID Judge qwen.qwen3-32b-v1:0 Backup (escalation) openai.gpt-oss-120b-1:0 Open the Amazon Bedrock console, switch the Region to Asia Pacific (Sydney), and make sure both models can be used by your account. If your console still shows a Model access page, request access to both models there.
You can check access from the CLI once your credentials are configured (step 5):
aws bedrock-runtime converse --region ap-southeast-2 \ --model-id qwen.qwen3-32b-v1:0 \ --messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"Xin chao"}]}]' A JSON answer with an output.message field means the model is reachable. An AccessDeniedException means access is not granted yet.
3. IAM permissions for the person who deploys The project repository does not ship a ready-made deploy policy. infra/README.md (§8.2) lists the minimum permission groups for the SAM stack:
CloudFormation: cloudformation:* on the stack askfirst-dev. Lambda: lambda:CreateFunction, lambda:DeleteFunction, lambda:UpdateFunction*, lambda:AddPermission, lambda:CreateFunctionUrlConfig, lambda:GetFunctionUrlConfig. IAM: iam:CreateRole, iam:DeleteRole, iam:GetRole, iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:DetachRolePolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy, iam:DeleteRolePolicy, iam:PassRole (on the roles SAM creates for the functions). DynamoDB: dynamodb:CreateTable, dynamodb:DeleteTable, dynamodb:DescribeTable, dynamodb:UpdateTimeToLive, dynamodb:UpdateContinuousBackups. SQS: sqs:CreateQueue, sqs:DeleteQueue, sqs:GetQueueAttributes, sqs:SetQueueAttributes. S3: s3:CreateBucket, s3:DeleteBucket, s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock, s3:PutEncryptionConfiguration, s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration, s3:PutObject, s3:DeleteObject. SSM: ssm:PutParameter, ssm:DeleteParameter, ssm:GetParameter*, and kms:Decrypt (to read SecureString values with --with-decryption). The current template and the AI steps also need the following. These are derived from infra/template.yaml, infra/github-oidc.yaml and ai/scripts/create_guardrail.py, not from a policy the team tested:
Lambda (versions, alias, SQS trigger): lambda:PublishVersion, lambda:CreateAlias, lambda:UpdateAlias, lambda:DeleteAlias, lambda:CreateEventSourceMapping, lambda:UpdateEventSourceMapping, lambda:DeleteEventSourceMapping, lambda:GetFunction*. CloudWatch: cloudwatch:PutMetricAlarm, cloudwatch:DeleteAlarms, cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms. ECR and OIDC (5.4): ecr:CreateRepository, ecr:PutLifecyclePolicy, ecr:DeleteRepository, ecr:DescribeImages, ecr:BatchGetImage, ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer, iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider. Bedrock (5.4): bedrock:CreateGuardrail, bedrock:CreateGuardrailVersion, bedrock:ListGuardrails, bedrock:InvokeModel. SAM artifact bucket: resolve_s3 = true in samconfig.toml makes SAM create a managed stack (aws-sam-cli-managed-default) with an S3 bucket for build artifacts the first time you deploy. Do not use the root user. Prefer short-lived credentials (IAM Identity Center / aws configure sso) over long-lived access keys. Never commit credentials to Git.
4. Tools to install Tool Version used by the project Check Notes Git any recent git --version GitHub account + GitHub CLI gh any recent gh --version You need your own fork of the repository so GitHub Actions can build the AI image in your account (5.4). Java JDK 21 (CI uses Temurin 21) java -version Runtime of webhook and worker is java21. Apache Maven wrapper pins 3.10.0 ./mvnw -v The repo ships mvnw/mvnw.cmd. AWS CLI v2 aws --version AWS SAM CLI 1.100+ sam --version Windows: winget install --id Amazon.SAM-CLI --exact Python 3.12 (requires-python = ">=3.12") python3 --version For the Telegram scripts and the AI scripts. uv any recent uv --version Python package manager used in ai/ (CI installs Python 3.12 through uv). OpenSSL any openssl version Only to generate a random webhook secret. Docker any recent docker --version Optional. Only for building the AI image locally (option B in 5.4). The normal path builds it on GitHub Actions. 5. Configure AWS credentials aws configure # or: aws configure sso # Default region name: ap-southeast-1 # Default output format: json aws sts get-caller-identity The last command must print your account (<ACCOUNT_ID>) and the identity you will deploy with.
6. Fork and clone the repository Fork the project repository on GitHub into your own account or organisation, then clone your fork:
git clone https://github.com/<GITHUB_OWNER>/<REPO>.git ask-first cd ask-first All later commands start from this repository root unless a step says otherwise.
7. Create the Telegram bot with BotFather In Telegram, open a chat with @BotFather (check the blue verification tick). Send /newbot. Enter a display name, for example Hoi Truoc Dev. Enter a username that ends with bot, for example <BOT_USERNAME> (it must be unique on Telegram). BotFather replies with an HTTP API token of the form <BOT_ID>:<SECRET_PART>. This is <TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN> in the rest of this guide. The bot token gives full control of the bot. Keep it only in a password manager and in SSM Parameter Store (5.5). Do not paste it into chats, screenshots, Git or samconfig.toml. If it leaks, send /revoke to BotFather and store the new token.
When everything above is ready, continue with 5.3 Deploy the infrastructure.

title: Proposal
content:
Ask First (“Hỏi Trước”) A serverless Telegram assistant that helps elderly people check suspected scam messages before they act 1. Overview Ask First is a Telegram bot for elderly people in Vietnam. When they receive a suspicious message, link or screenshot, they forward it to the bot. The bot answers in plain Vietnamese with:
one of 4 risk levels: DANGEROUS, SUSPICIOUS, UNSURE, LOW_RISK (there is deliberately no “safe” level), the scam scenario it resembles, the warning signs quoted from the message itself, what to do right now, and a verified official hotline, an optional alert to a family member who was linked with the elderly person’s explicit consent, when the risk is high. The bot plays the role of the “third person” who steps in before the money leaves the account. It runs fully serverless on AWS: Java 21 Lambdas handle Telegram and orchestration, a Python 3.12 Lambda runs the AI pipeline (local OCR, rules, local RAG), and only the final “judge” step calls an open-weight LLM on Amazon Bedrock with text that has already been masked.
Item Value Team 4 people: 2 backend (Java 21), 2 AI (Python 3.12) Timeframe 6 weeks, 19/10/2026 – 29/11/2026 (FCAJ bootcamp) Regions Compute in ap-southeast-1 (Singapore); Bedrock in ap-southeast-2 (Sydney) Channel Telegram Bot API (webhook) Estimated cost ≈ 6.2 USD/month for 3,000 checks without Free Tier, ≈ 2.4 USD/month with always-free tiers (section 6) 2. Problem statement Online scams are large-scale in Vietnam, and elderly people are a main target.
The Ministry of Public Security estimated losses from online fraud in 2025 at more than 8,000 billion VND (VOV). In the 2025 survey of the National Cybersecurity Association (NCA), impersonating the police was the most common scam type, and only 32.12% of victims reported to the authorities (Báo Hải Phòng, Công Lý). Thai Nguyen police reported that victims of the “fake police officer” scenario are “mainly elderly people and people in remote areas” (Bộ Công an). The gap. Banks already warn at transfer time, but the decisive manipulation happens earlier: scammers isolate the victim (“do not talk to anyone”). In the cases where a scam was stopped, a third person (bank teller, post office staff, local police) stepped in before the transfer. Elderly people have no simple tool to forward a screenshot or link and get an explanation they understand, and their children are often not there.
Target users
User Need Elderly person (primary) Forward / screenshot / paste a suspicious message, get a short, clear answer within seconds, no app to install Family member (secondary) Be alerted when a linked elderly relative receives a high-risk message, with one “I have contacted them” button 3. Goals and scope Success criteria (set before building; source: architecture doc §1.3, plan §4):
Criterion Target Scam recall ≥ 90% False positives on “benign but suspicious-looking” messages ≤ 10% End-to-end latency (warm) p95 ≤ 15 s for text and images Cost ≤ 0.005 USD per check; ≤ 50 USD/month at demo scale Privacy Images stay in the ai Lambda’s memory; the LLM only sees masked text; logs contain no message content; all user data has a TTL In scope (MVP, 6 weeks)
Text, links (including links hidden behind text), screenshots and albums, forwarded messages; several messages sent in a row are grouped into one answer. 4-level verdict with scenario, signs, actions, official hotline and a citation from official warnings (RAG). Onboarding with explicit consent, withdraw consent, delete data. Family linking (double opt-in), family alerts, 15-minute reminder, “I have contacted them” acknowledgement. In-chat management: /nguoithan, /lichsu, /rutdongy, /xoadulieu, /caidat; “first 30 minutes” checklist after being scammed (/bilua). “Bot was wrong” feedback button; kill switch to fall back to rules-only without redeploying; unsupported input handling (video, sticker, .apk…). Cut from the original plan to fit 6 weeks (plan v3, 19/10/2026 – the original plan was 12 weeks):
Cut / postponed Why Voice notes and local speech recognition (ASR) Time; the bot replies “voice is not supported yet” VLM fallback for hard images Time; local OCR passed its gate (section 4) Multi-turn follow-up questions Time Telegram Mini App (web UI) Everything is done in chat with commands and inline buttons instead Phase 2: live knowledge base, “trending scams” page Out of the 6-week window Pilot with 10–20 households Replaced by internal testing with the team and their families; no real-user metrics outside the team Out of scope by design: blocking calls or transfers, a public blacklist of phone numbers or accounts, real-time deepfake video detection, sending SMS, recording calls.
4. Solution architecture Design principles
Serverless, event-driven, no VPC and no NAT – small, uneven load; pay per request; avoids a fixed NAT cost of about 32 USD/month. Hybrid local-first AI – OCR, PII masking, rules and embeddings run on CPU inside Lambda. Only the judge step calls Bedrock, and only with masked text. Controlled workflow, not an agent – Normalize → Extract → Mask PII → Signals (rules + URL) → Retrieve (RAG) → Guard → Judge → Fuse → Respond. The rules layer works without the LLM, so the bot always answers. Store no original content – only verdict, signal codes and hashes, with a 30-day TTL. AWS services and why each was chosen
Service Role Why this service AWS Lambda – webhook, worker, worker-dlq (Java 21, zip) Receive Telegram updates via Function URL, orchestrate checks, send replies and family alerts Pay per invocation; Function URL gives an HTTPS endpoint without API Gateway AWS Lambda – ai (Python 3.12, container image, 3008 MB) Whole AI pipeline with local models (OCR, embeddings) Container image fits ML libraries beyond the 250 MB zip limit; images are processed in memory only Amazon SQS + DLQ Queue between webhook and worker Webhook returns 200 immediately; caps concurrency to protect Bedrock quota; free retries; DelaySeconds implements message grouping (3 s) and the 15-minute reminder without a scheduler Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand, single table) Users, consent, family links, check metadata, dedup, cache, rate limit, feature flags Key-value access, TTL for data minimisation, conditional writes for idempotency, PITR enabled Amazon Bedrock – Qwen3 32B (judge), gpt-oss-120b (backup) Structured classification of masked text Serverless, pay per token, no GPU to run. Open-weight models are available in-region in Sydney, not in Singapore Amazon Bedrock Guardrails PROMPT_ATTACK filter on input Detects prompt injection inside the forwarded message Amazon S3 Local model weights, RAG index, eval sets, voluntarily donated samples (donated/ expires after 30 days) Cheap; swap models without rebuilding the image; Block Public Access + SSE Amazon ECR Stores the ai container image Required for image-based Lambda SSM Parameter Store (SecureString) Bot token, webhook secret, stack config No secrets in code or Lambda environment variables CloudWatch + SNS Logs (JSON, shared trace_id), DLQ alarm → email to the team Alarm needs a target; SNS is used only for internal alarms IAM + GitHub Actions OIDC Least-privilege roles (the ai role may only touch CACHE# / URL# keys); CI/CD without stored access keys Security by default Deliberately not used: API Gateway (Function URL is enough), Step Functions (linear pipeline under 30 s), OpenSearch / vector DB (small corpus, cosine in memory, RAG p95 45 ms on Lambda), EC2/SageMaker GPU (far more expensive than per-token Bedrock at this scale), Amazon Transcribe (voice postponed), Textract, Bedrock Agents, VPC/NAT.
Main data flow (summary; the diagram numbers 17 detailed steps)
The elderly person forwards a message; Telegram POSTs the update to the webhook Function URL with a secret_token (checked in constant time). webhook deduplicates the update_id, checks consent, buffers the message (BUFFER#), sends “⏳ checking…”, and puts a job on SQS with a 3 s delay. It answers Telegram in under 1 s. worker reads the buffer and the kill-switch flags, then invokes ai synchronously with op=analyze (metadata and file_id only, never image bytes). ai downloads the image straight into memory, runs OCR and local models, masks phone numbers, account numbers, ID numbers, OTPs and emails, applies rules and URL checks, and retrieves scenario cards (RAG). ai calls Bedrock Guardrails, then the judge (Qwen3 32B; gpt-oss-120b on low confidence or error), fuses rule and LLM scores into a level, and renders the Vietnamese answer from a template. If the level is DANGEROUS with a risky action, worker alerts all linked family members in parallel; the “already alerted” state is recorded only after Telegram returns a message_id. worker edits the “⏳” message into the final answer and writes CHECK# metadata (TTL 30 days); a 15-minute reminder is scheduled if no family member acknowledged. A job that fails 5 times goes to the DLQ: worker-dlq tells the user the bot is busy, and the CloudWatch alarm on the DLQ emails the team through SNS. Configuration details of the deployed dev stack (infra/template.yaml): SQS maximum concurrency is 5 for worker and 2 for worker-dlq; SnapStart is a parameter that is off by default until cold starts are measured (ADR-008); the OCR model is RapidOCR PP-OCRv6 small. VietOCR was enabled next to RapidOCR on 24/11/2026.
5. Plan and timeline Six one-week sprints, three parallel tracks (backend, AI, shared) joined by a JSON Schema contract between Java and Python.

6. Budget estimation Load assumption: 3,000 checks/month, text and images, no voice. Non-Bedrock services were priced with the AWS Pricing Calculator (created 24/11/2026, ap-southeast-1, “Without Free Tier”). Bedrock was calculated by hand because the Calculator does not offer Qwen3 in Sydney; token counts were measured on the real pipeline.

Per check, LLM tokens only: ≈ 0.000792 USD (≈ 20 VND), well under the 0.005 USD target. The 2,250 LLM calls assume 25% of checks are answered by the rules fast path or cache. This ratio is not verified: the eval set is almost all scams and hard cases. If every check calls the LLM, Bedrock is ≈ 2.7 USD/month. Checked against real numbers (25/11/2026, team dev account, free APIs only)
Free Tier: the account still gets the always-free tiers. November up to 25/11: Lambda ≈ 8,200/400,000 GB-seconds and 273/1M requests, SQS ≈ 178,000/1M requests, CloudWatch alarms 0.37/10. The “With always-free” column holds for this account. Lambda durations (CloudWatch Duration, 14 days, team test traffic): ai 248 invocations, avg 2.7 s, p95 9.7 s; worker 73, avg 4.6 s, p95 14.2 s; webhook 50, avg 1.0 s, p95 3.0 s. ai and worker fit within the 5 s entered in the Calculator. webhook runs twice the assumed 0.5 s, so that line becomes about 0.06 USD without Free Tier; the total barely moves. Small sample of test traffic, not real load. Actual spend, dev account: AWS Budgets shows ≈ 0.09 USD for November up to 25/11, forecast ≈ 0.10 USD for the month (Bedrock not included). Actual spend, Bedrock account (Cost Explorer, 01–25/11): 3.93 USD in total, of which 3.57 USD is Bedrock and 0.36 USD is tax (≈ 10%). Qwen3 32B: 11.8M input tokens, 0.94M output tokens = 2.40 USD. gpt-oss-120b (fallback): 2.5M input tokens, 0.44M output tokens = 0.66 USD. Most of these calls are the team’s eval and test runs, not real users. Tax: the bill adds ≈ 10% tax that the estimate above does not include (the Pricing Calculator does not include tax either). Cost optimisation
No VPC/NAT, no API Gateway, no OpenSearch, no GPU – avoids every fixed monthly cost; the bill scales with use. Local-first AI – OCR, embeddings and rules run inside Lambda at no per-token cost; only the judge calls Bedrock with a cheap open-weight model. Fast path and cache – each check that skips the LLM saves ≈ 0.00094 USD (tokens + Guardrails). Kill switch (CONFIG#global/FLAGS) – turns off the LLM judge or image intake without a redeploy if a cost alarm fires or the bot is spammed; per-user rate limit caps abuse. Free Tier – Lambda, SQS and CloudWatch fit in the always-free tiers at this load (6.2 → 2.4 USD). Retention and lifecycle – S3 donated/ already expires after 30 days. title: Blog 3
content:
Designing a cost-optimized IoT data pipeline (MQTT → AWS IoT Core → Glue → S3) for small projects Post link: AWS Study Group
Author(s): Ngô Thị Kim Ngân · Published: November 27, 2026
Summary The post covers how IoT devices that keep sending small JSON messages pile millions of files into S3, which drives up request costs and slows Athena queries. The serverless fix has two stages: the IoT Core Rule Engine writes raw data straight to S3 in time partitions, and a daily Glue job merges the files and converts them to Parquet. Raw files are deleted after 7 days by an S3 Lifecycle rule.
Key points Use the IoT Core Rule Engine (filtering with SQL) to write directly to S3 under raw-data/year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/hour=HH/..., with no EC2 or Lambda in between. EventBridge Scheduler runs a Glue job at the end of each day: it reads the previous day’s JSON, cleans the data types, merges it and writes Snappy-compressed Parquet to a curated bucket. An S3 Lifecycle rule deletes raw JSON after 7 days, which still leaves enough for debugging. By the post’s own estimate (10 million messages a month): storage drops by about 85%, file count goes from 10 million to about 30, and the data Athena scans to read one column drops by about 98%. For small data, use Glue Python Shell with awswrangler instead of Spark. With Spark, choose G.1X workers and cap them at 2.

title: Deploy the infrastructure
content:
In this step you build the Java backend and deploy the SAM stack askfirst-dev. At the end you will have the webhook, worker and worker-dlq functions, the DynamoDB table, the SQS queue and DLQ, the S3 bucket, the SSM configuration parameters and the DLQ alarm. The ai function is added in 5.4.
What the stack creates Resource Logical ID in infra/template.yaml Name on AWS Lambda webhook (Java 21, public Function URL) WebhookFunction askfirst-dev-webhook Lambda worker (Java 21, SQS trigger, alias live) WorkerFunction askfirst-dev-worker Lambda for DLQ messages WorkerDlqFunction askfirst-dev-worker-dlq DynamoDB single table (PK/SK, GSI1, TTL ttl, PITR, on-demand) AskFirstTable askfirst-dev SQS queue (visibility 720 s, DLQ after 5 receives) JobsQueue askfirst-dev-jobs SQS dead-letter queue (14-day retention) JobsDeadLetterQueue askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq CloudWatch alarm on the DLQ JobsDlqAlarm askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty S3 bucket (Block Public Access, SSE, donated/ expires after 30 days) DataBucket askfirst-dev-data-<ACCOUNT_ID> SSM parameters (stage, table name, queue URLs, bucket name) StageParam, TableNameParam, JobsQueueUrlParam, JobsDlqUrlParam, DataBucketNameParam /askfirst/dev/... Lambda ai (container image) AiFunction askfirst-dev-ai, only created when AiImageUri is set (5.4) There is no VPC and no NAT Gateway: Lambda reaches DynamoDB, SQS, S3 and the Internet without them.
Step 1: Set common shell variables Run from the repository root:
export AWS_REGION=ap-southeast-1 export STAGE=dev Step 2: Build the Java backend sam build builds each function directory on its own, so the shared module common must first be installed into your local Maven repository:
cd backend/ScamProtection ./mvnw clean install -DskipTests cd ../.. On Windows PowerShell use .\mvnw.cmd clean install -DskipTests.
The output should end with BUILD SUCCESS.
Step 3: Create the privacy-policy hash parameter The template reads /askfirst/<stage>/config/policy_sha256 at deploy time ({{resolve:ssm:...}} in POLICY_SHA256), so this parameter must exist before the first sam deploy. It is not a secret: it is the version of the privacy policy that users accept in the bot. When the policy file changes, the hash changes and users are asked to accept again.
POLICY_SHA=$(shasum -a 256 docs/privacy-policy.md | cut -d' ' -f1) # or: sha256sum aws ssm put-parameter --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/config/policy_sha256" \ --value "$POLICY_SHA" --type String --overwrite Step 4: Build the SAM application cd infra sam build SAM reads infra/template.yaml, builds the Java 21 functions from backend/ScamProtection/webhook-handler/ and backend/ScamProtection/worker/, and writes the result to infra/.aws-sam/build. The output should end with Build Succeeded.
Step 5: Deploy the stack infra/samconfig.toml already contains the deploy settings for dev: stack_name = "askfirst-dev", region = "ap-southeast-1", capabilities = "CAPABILITY_IAM", resolve_s3 = true, confirm_changeset = false.
The worker and worker-dlq functions receive the bot token through the NoEcho template parameter TelegramBotToken. Read it into a shell variable without echoing it, so it does not land in your shell history:
read -rs TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN # paste <TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN>, then press Enter export TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN Deploy (still inside infra/):
sam deploy --parameter-overrides \ Stage="$STAGE" \ TelegramBotToken="$TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" \ TelegramBotUsername="<BOT_USERNAME>" TelegramBotUsername is the bot username without @. It is optional and only used to build invitation deep links for relatives. Do not write the token into samconfig.toml. --parameter-overrides on the command line replaces the parameter_overrides line of samconfig.toml, so always pass Stage too. Pass the same full set of parameters on every later deploy (after 5.4 this includes AiImageUri): if AiImageUri ends up empty, the template condition HasAiImage is false and CloudFormation removes the ai function.
If you prefer to review each setting, run sam deploy --guided instead and answer: Stack Name askfirst-dev, Region ap-southeast-1, Parameter Stage dev, Allow SAM CLI IAM role creation Y, “WebhookFunction has no authentication. Is this okay?” Y (the Function URL must be public; the secret header is checked inside the function), Save arguments to configuration file Y.
Step 6: Read the stack outputs aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$AWS_REGION" --stack-name askfirst-dev \ --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[].[OutputKey,OutputValue]" --output table Keep these values for the next steps: WebhookFunctionUrl (5.5), DataBucketName (5.4), JobsQueueUrl, JobsDlqUrl, WorkerRoleArn.
export FUNCTION_URL=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$AWS_REGION" --stack-name askfirst-dev \ --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='WebhookFunctionUrl'].OutputValue" --output text) export DATA_BUCKET=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$AWS_REGION" --stack-name askfirst-dev \ --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='DataBucketName'].OutputValue" --output text) echo "$FUNCTION_URL" "$DATA_BUCKET" Step 7: Check the resources These commands only read. They come from infra/README.md §4.
# DynamoDB: on-demand, PK/SK, GSI1, ACTIVE aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name askfirst-dev --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --query "Table.[TableName,BillingModeSummary.BillingMode,KeySchema,GlobalSecondaryIndexes[0].IndexName,TableStatus]" # TTL on attribute "ttl" and PITR enabled aws dynamodb describe-time-to-live --table-name askfirst-dev --region "$AWS_REGION" aws dynamodb describe-continuous-backups --table-name askfirst-dev --region "$AWS_REGION" # S3: all four Block Public Access flags true, lifecycle on donated/ aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket "$DATA_BUCKET" --region "$AWS_REGION" aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket "$DATA_BUCKET" --region "$AWS_REGION" # SQS: VisibilityTimeout 720 and RedrivePolicy to the DLQ with maxReceiveCount 5 aws sqs get-queue-attributes --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --queue-url "$(aws ssm get-parameter --region "$AWS_REGION" --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/sqs/jobs_queue_url" --query Parameter.Value --output text)" \ --attribute-names VisibilityTimeout RedrivePolicy # SSM: configuration parameters written by the stack aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --region "$AWS_REGION" --path "/askfirst/$STAGE" --recursive \ --query "Parameters[*].[Name,Type]" --output table The webhook itself is checked in 5.5, after the bot token and webhook secret are stored in SSM; until then the webhook function cannot start.
Troubleshooting Symptom Cause and fix Deploy fails on POLICY_SHA256 / parameter not found Step 3 was skipped or used another Region. Create /askfirst/dev/config/policy_sha256 in ap-southeast-1 and deploy again. Stack is in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE after the first deploy CloudFormation cannot update it. Run sam delete --stack-name askfirst-dev, fix the cause, deploy again. S3 Bucket already exists Bucket names are global; the name contains your account ID, so check that you are deploying to the right account (aws sts get-caller-identity). AccessDenied on IAM actions The deploying identity is missing permissions from 5.2. To see why a resource failed:
aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --region "$AWS_REGION" --stack-name askfirst-dev \ --query "StackEvents[?ResourceStatus=='CREATE_FAILED'].[LogicalResourceId,ResourceStatusReason]" \ --output table Next: 5.4 Deploy the AI function.

title: Deploy the AI function
content:
The ai function is a Python container image Lambda (3008 MB, timeout 90 s, 1 GB /tmp, x86_64, alias live). It runs OCR, PII masking, rules, retrieval from the knowledge base, Bedrock Guardrails and the Bedrock judge. In this step you:
create an ECR repository and a GitHub OIDC role (once per account), (optional) create your own Bedrock Guardrail, upload the model weights and the knowledge-base index to S3, build and push the image with GitHub Actions, deploy the stack again with AiImageUri, and test the function. Model files are not inside the image. On cold start the function downloads them from the data bucket into /tmp and checks their SHA-256 against ai/config/artifacts.yaml.
Run every command from the repository root unless stated otherwise, with the variables from 5.3 set (AWS_REGION, STAGE, DATA_BUCKET, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN).
Step 1: Create the ECR repository and the GitHub OIDC role infra/github-oidc.yaml creates:
the ECR repository askfirst-ai (keeps the 5 newest images), the IAM role askfirst-github-ai-image, which GitHub Actions assumes through OIDC to push images. It can only push to that repository, and only from the repository named in the GitHubRepo parameter, the GitHub OIDC identity provider (skip it with CreateOidcProvider=false if your account already has one). The GitHubRepo parameter defaults to the team repository. On your fork, pass your own <GITHUB_OWNER>/<REPO>, otherwise your workflow cannot assume the role:
aws cloudformation deploy --region ap-southeast-1 --stack-name askfirst-github-oidc \ --template-file infra/github-oidc.yaml --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM \ --parameter-overrides GitHubRepo=<GITHUB_OWNER>/<REPO> # add CreateOidcProvider=false to --parameter-overrides if the GitHub OIDC provider already exists Store the role ARN as a repository variable of your fork (a variable, not a secret: the ARN alone grants nothing):
gh variable set AWS_AI_IMAGE_ROLE_ARN --body "$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region ap-southeast-1 \ --stack-name askfirst-github-oidc \ --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='AiImagePushRoleArn'].OutputValue" --output text)" gh uses the repository of the current clone. Add --repo <GITHUB_OWNER>/<REPO> if it points elsewhere.
Step 2 (optional): Create your own Bedrock Guardrail The guardrail.id in ai/config/models.yaml belongs to the team’s Bedrock account, so it will not work in yours. Without a working guardrail the pipeline skips the guardrail check and still runs. To enable it in your account (Region ap-southeast-2):
cd ai uv run python scripts/create_guardrail.py --dry-run # print the request only uv run python scripts/create_guardrail.py # create guardrail "askfirst-guard" cd .. The script prints a line of the form guardrail: {id: "<GUARDRAIL_ID>", version: "<VERSION>", ...}. Put <GUARDRAIL_ID> and <VERSION> into the guardrail: line of ai/config/models.yaml. This file is baked into the image, so this edit must be committed before step 4.
Step 3: Upload model files and the knowledge-base index to S3 The function reads four artifacts. Their versions, S3 prefixes and SHA-256 are fixed in ai/config/artifacts.yaml:
Artifact S3 prefix How to get it ocr ocr/ppocrv6-small-rapidocr3.10.0/ scripts/fetch_ocr_models.py (RapidOCR PP-OCRv6 small, ONNX fp32) embedder embedder/e5-small-qint8-614241f/ scripts/fetch_embedder.py (multilingual-e5-small, int8 ONNX) kb_index kb_index/kb-2026.11.11/ scripts/build_index.py from kb/scenarios.yaml and kb/alerts.yaml vietocr vietocr/vgg-seq2seq-0.3.13-fp32/ Optional. scripts/export_vietocr_onnx.py needs a separate PyTorch environment (see the script header). Download and build them (inside ai/):
cd ai uv run python scripts/fetch_ocr_models.py out/ocr uv run python scripts/fetch_embedder.py out/embedder uv run python scripts/build_index.py out/embedder out/kb_index --version kb-2026.11.11 fetch_* stop if a downloaded file does not match artifacts.yaml. build_index.py prints the SHA-256 of index.npy and meta.json. According to ai/MODELS.md, a different machine can produce slightly different floats. If the printed SHA-256 differ from the kb_index entry in ai/config/artifacts.yaml, write your values there (and commit before step 4), because the function checks them on load.
Upload (still inside ai/):
export ARTIFACT_BUCKET="$DATA_BUCKET" uv run python scripts/upload_artifacts.py ocr out/ocr uv run python scripts/upload_artifacts.py embedder out/embedder uv run python scripts/upload_artifacts.py kb_index out/kb_index cd .. upload_artifacts.py checks every file against artifacts.yaml first and uploads nothing if one does not match. Each uploaded key is printed as đã upload s3://<bucket>/<key>.
If you skip vietocr, OCR still works with RapidOCR alone: the function logs ocr_reread_failed once and continues.
Step 4: Build and push the image with GitHub Actions The image is built on GitHub Actions, not on your laptop (.github/workflows/ai-image.yml). Commit and push any change from steps 2 and 3 to main of your fork first.
GitHub disables workflows on a new fork. Open the Actions tab of your fork once and enable them.
Start the workflow from the UI (Actions → AI image → Run workflow, branch main) or from the CLI:
gh workflow run ai-image.yml --ref main gh run watch The workflow builds ai/Dockerfile from the repository root, checks that the image is at most 2 GB, imports all libraries on a read-only root filesystem, calls the handler once in stub mode through the Lambda Runtime Interface Emulator, and then (only on a manual run) assumes the OIDC role and pushes:
<ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/askfirst-ai:<GIT_SHA> The run summary prints the full URI in a line Deploy: sam deploy --parameter-overrides AiImageUri=<URI> .... You can also list the images:
aws ecr describe-images --region ap-southeast-1 --repository-name askfirst-ai \ --query "sort_by(imageDetails,&imagePushedAt)[-1].imageTags" --output text export AI_IMAGE_URI="<ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/askfirst-ai:<GIT_SHA>" Step 5: Deploy the stack with the AI image Go back to infra/ and deploy with the full parameter set from 5.3 plus AiImageUri:
cd infra sam deploy --parameter-overrides \ Stage="$STAGE" \ TelegramBotToken="$TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" \ TelegramBotUsername="<BOT_USERNAME>" \ AiImageUri="$AI_IMAGE_URI" cd .. CloudFormation now creates askfirst-dev-ai with alias live. The worker already calls askfirst-dev-ai:live.
If the real pipeline fails and you need the bot running end to end first, deploy again with AiPipelineImpl=stub added. The stub answers from fixed keyword rules, with no media download and no network calls (no OCR, no Bedrock). It is meant for the dev bot only. Remove it (or set AiPipelineImpl=real) when the real pipeline works.
Step 6: Test the AI function Invoke the alias with the analyze fixture used by CI (text “Chào bạn”):
python3 -c "import json; print(json.dumps(json.load(open('contracts/fixtures/analyze/default.json'))['request']))" > req.json aws lambda invoke --region ap-southeast-1 --function-name askfirst-dev-ai:live \ --payload fileb://req.json out.json python3 -c "import json,sys; r=json.load(open('out.json')); sys.exit(0 if r.get('op')=='analyze' and not r.get('error') and r.get('analyze') else 1)" \ && echo OK || cat out.json rm -f req.json aws lambda invoke should print "StatusCode": 200, and the check prints OK when the response has op = analyze, no error, and an analyze object. The first call is a cold start: the team measured an init time of about 6.2 s at p50 for this function (source: docs/results/lambda-p95.md), plus model downloads from S3.
Read the logs if it fails:
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-ai --region ap-southeast-1 --since 10m Optional: Bedrock in another AWS account Skip this if Bedrock is enabled in the same account as the Lambda functions (the normal case for this guide). The team ran Lambda in one account and Bedrock in another. If the ai function has the environment variable BEDROCK_ROLE_ARN, it assumes that role before calling Bedrock (ai/src/askfirst/llm/bedrock.py). Otherwise it calls Bedrock in its own account.
Find the name of the ai function’s execution role (the last part of the ARN):
aws lambda get-function-configuration --region ap-southeast-1 \ --function-name askfirst-dev-ai --query Role --output text In the Bedrock account:
aws iam create-role --role-name askfirst-bedrock-from-team --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::<TEAM_ACCOUNT>:role/<AI_LAMBDA_ROLE>"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}' aws iam put-role-policy --role-name askfirst-bedrock-from-team --policy-name bedrock --policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["bedrock:InvokeModel","bedrock:ApplyGuardrail"],"Resource":"*"}]}' In the Lambda account:
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name <AI_LAMBDA_ROLE> --policy-name assume-bedrock --policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"sts:AssumeRole","Resource":"arn:aws:iam::<BEDROCK_ACCOUNT>:role/askfirst-bedrock-from-team"}]}' Then set BEDROCK_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::<BEDROCK_ACCOUNT>:role/askfirst-bedrock-from-team on the ai function.
In the team’s dev environment, BEDROCK_ROLE_ARN is set on both $LATEST and the live alias of the ai function (checked 25/11/2026), but neither the template nor the CI workflow defines it, so it was set outside the repo. The next sam deploy may wipe it. The live alias points to a published version, so after changing $LATEST you must publish a new version and update the alias. An inline policy attached to the SAM-generated role can also be lost if CloudFormation replaces the role. Re-check the variable and the policy after every deploy.

title: Connect Telegram
content:
In this last deployment step you store the bot secrets in SSM Parameter Store, check that the webhook rejects requests without the secret, register the webhook with Telegram, set the bot menu and send the first message.
Run every command from the repository root with the variables from 5.3 set (AWS_REGION, STAGE, FUNCTION_URL, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN).
Step 1: Store the bot token and webhook secret in SSM The webhook and ai functions read two SecureString parameters from SSM (webhook at init, ai on first use), so no redeploy is needed after you create them:
SSM parameter Type Read by Notes /askfirst/dev/telegram/bot_token SecureString webhook (TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN_PARAM), ai (BOT_TOKEN_PARAM) The token from BotFather /askfirst/dev/telegram/webhook_secret SecureString webhook (TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET_PARAM) Only A-Za-z0-9_-, at most 256 characters /askfirst/dev/config/policy_sha256 String CloudFormation at deploy time Already created in 5.3 Generate a random webhook secret and store both values. The values never appear on screen or in your shell history:
# Bot token: reuses $TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN from 5.3 (otherwise: read -rs TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN) aws ssm put-parameter --region "$AWS_REGION" --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/telegram/bot_token" \ --value "$TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" --type SecureString --overwrite # Webhook secret: 64 hex characters TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) aws ssm put-parameter --region "$AWS_REGION" --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/telegram/webhook_secret" \ --value "$TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET" --type SecureString --overwrite export TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET PowerShell versions of these commands (with Read-Host) are in infra/README.md §5.
Check the types: both Telegram parameters must be SecureString, policy_sha256 must be String:
aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --region "$AWS_REGION" --path "/askfirst/$STAGE" --recursive \ --query "Parameters[*].[Name,Type]" --output table Never print these values, put them in screenshots or commit them. --with-decryption shows the plaintext, so use it only inside a command substitution as below. If a token or secret leaks, revoke the token with BotFather (/revoke), store the new values and repeat steps 1 and 3.
Step 2: Check the webhook authentication The Function URL is public (AuthType: NONE), so the function itself must reject any request without the correct X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header.
# No secret: expect 401 curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$FUNCTION_URL" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}' # Correct secret, empty update: expect "IGNORED" then 200 curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$FUNCTION_URL" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: $TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET" -d '{}' You can also run the read-only check script, which tests both cases and the resources from 5.3. It prints [PASS] or [FAIL] per item and exits with code 1 on any failure:
./infra/verify-dev.sh ap-southeast-1 dev Actual output on the dev environment (25/11/2026), no-secret case:
$ curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$FUNCTION_URL" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}' UNAUTHORIZED 401 Step 3: Register the webhook with Telegram scripts/set_webhook.py calls the Telegram Bot API setWebhook with the Function URL and the secret, subscribes to the updates message, callback_query and my_chat_member, then prints getWebhookInfo. It reads TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET from the environment (exported above). It refuses to register a webhook without a secret.
python3 scripts/set_webhook.py --url "$FUNCTION_URL" Check the printed block: URL must equal your WebhookFunctionUrl, Allowed updates must list the three update types, and there must be no Lỗi gần nhất từ Telegram (last error from Telegram) line.
Other options: --drop-pending discards updates Telegram queued while the webhook was down; --delete removes the webhook.
Step 4: Set the bot menu python3 scripts/set_commands.py This sets the Telegram menu commands /batdau, /huongdan, /caidat, /nguoithan, /lichsu and /bilua. It is safe to run again.
Step 5: Send the first message Open the chat with your bot in Telegram (search for <BOT_USERNAME>) and press Start (or send /batdau). The bot replies with a welcome and privacy-consent message and a ✅ Đồng ý button. Press it. Until you agree, the bot does not check any message. Send or forward a suspicious text, for example a fake prize message with a link. The bot answers at once with a message starting with “⏳”. A few seconds later the same message is edited into the result: risk level, the matching scam scenario, the reasons, and what to do now. Send a screenshot of a suspicious message to test OCR. The first image after a deploy is slower because the ai function downloads its models from S3. Feature flags live in the DynamoDB item CONFIG#global / FLAGS. If the item does not exist, the defaults are llm_enabled=true, feature_image=true, feature_voice=false, feature_rag=true, so nothing has to be created for this test.
Troubleshooting Follow the logs of each function while you send a message:
sam logs -n WebhookFunction --stack-name askfirst-dev --region "$AWS_REGION" --tail sam logs -n WorkerFunction --stack-name askfirst-dev --region "$AWS_REGION" --tail sam logs -n AiFunction --stack-name askfirst-dev --region "$AWS_REGION" --tail Symptom Where to look Bot does not answer at all Run set_webhook.py again and read Lỗi gần nhất từ Telegram. A 401 there means the secret in SSM differs from the one registered: repeat step 3 with the value stored in SSM. webhook logs show an SSM error A parameter from step 1 is missing, has the wrong name or the wrong Region. “⏳” appears but is never edited The job reached SQS but the worker or ai failed: read the worker and ai logs. After 5 failed attempts the job goes to askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq, worker-dlq tells the user the bot is busy, and the alarm askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty goes to ALARM. ai errors about artifacts or SHA-256 A file in S3 does not match ai/config/artifacts.yaml (see 5.4, step 3). ai errors from Bedrock Model access in ap-southeast-2 (5.2) or the guardrail ID (5.4, step 2). To read the secret back from SSM without printing it, for example in a new shell:
export TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=$(aws ssm get-parameter --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/telegram/webhook_secret" --with-decryption \ --query Parameter.Value --output text) The worker and worker-dlq functions get the token from the deploy parameter TelegramBotToken (5.3), not from SSM. When you change the token, update SSM and deploy again with the new TelegramBotToken and the full parameter set, including AiImageUri.
The bot is now running end to end on AWS.

title: Workshop
content:
Ask First (“Hỏi Trước”): a serverless scam-check bot on AWS Overview Ask First is a Telegram bot that helps elderly people check a suspicious message before they act on it. The user forwards a text, a link or a screenshot to the bot. Within seconds the bot answers in plain Vietnamese: how risky the message is, which scam pattern it matches, and what to do next. If the risk is high, the bot can also alert a relative who has agreed to receive alerts.
The whole system is serverless and runs on AWS:
AWS Lambda (Java 21) receives Telegram updates through a Function URL (webhook) and processes jobs from Amazon SQS (worker), with a dead-letter queue for failed jobs. A third Lambda, ai, is a container image (Python 3.12) that runs OCR and embedding models on CPU, applies rules and RAG, and calls Amazon Bedrock (Qwen3 32B, with gpt-oss-120b as backup) behind Bedrock Guardrails. Amazon DynamoDB stores metadata with TTL, Amazon S3 stores model weights and the knowledge-base index, SSM Parameter Store holds the bot token and webhook secret, and Amazon CloudWatch collects logs and the DLQ alarm. Everything is defined as code with AWS SAM and deployed in ap-southeast-1 (Singapore); Bedrock is called in ap-southeast-2 (Sydney). In this workshop you will rebuild the same system in your own AWS account, step by step, and finish with a working bot you can chat with on Telegram.
Content Overview Prerequisites Deploy the infrastructure (SAM) Deploy the AI function Connect Telegram Testing and validation Monitoring Cost Clean up Demo and lessons learned

title: Self-evaluation
content:
During the First Cloud AI Journey internship I was the AI member (AI1) of the team project Ask First. I worked on the scam-check pipeline: choosing and measuring OCR, choosing the Bedrock judge model, building the eval set and the level thresholds, packaging the ai Lambda as a container image, and measuring latency and cost on AWS. The table below is my self-evaluation; the evidence comes from my worklog and the project repo.
No. Criterion Good Fair Average Comment / evidence 1 Professional knowledge ✅ Worked hands-on with Lambda container images, SQS, DynamoDB, Bedrock (Qwen3 32B, Guardrails), OCR and model evaluation. Each technical decision has an ADR with measurements (ADR-001, ADR-003, ADR-005). 2 Self-learning ✅ Learned Vietnamese OCR, prompting an LLM judge, measuring recall and false alarms, and packaging Lambda containers; most of this was new to me before the program. 3 Proactiveness ✅ Reran benchmarks on CI to check the dev-machine numbers, built a separate red-team set (34 samples), and wrote down the limits myself (134 samples instead of 300, no real samples yet). 4 Discipline ✅ Most work met its milestone, but gate G1 (choose the LLM) slipped from 30/10 to 11/11. PRs were often merged in bursts and the worklog was not kept daily. 5 Communication ✅ Mostly through issues, PRs and ADRs, with the BE ↔ AI contract v1.0 so both sides could work in parallel. I could flag schedule risks to the team earlier. 6 Teamwork ✅ Reviewed about 26 PRs from AI2 and BE in weeks 6–10; the contract ships a StubPipeline and fixtures so BE could write Java without waiting for the AI pipeline. 7 Problem solving ✅ Switched URL scoring from substring to boundary matching (#105); kept separate thresholds for the rules-only path when the new ones failed the CI eval gate; handled the ai Lambda’s 10 s INIT limit with a post-deploy warm-up (#185). 8 Contribution to the Workshop ✅ The AI pipeline, eval report, Lambda latency numbers and cost estimate (about 0.000753 USD in tokens per text check) are used directly in the Proposal and Workshop. Areas to improve Set criteria before measuring. The OCR CER ≤ 10% threshold was set after seeing the results. Next time I fix thresholds and scoring rules before running. Keep a steadier pace. Write the worklog daily, keep PRs small and merge them steadily, and raise a flag early when a gate may slip. Thin evaluation data. The eval set has only 134 samples and no real ones, and image end-to-end p95 is 17.0 s, above the 15 s target. These are the two things I would work on next.

title: Testing & Validation
content:
In this step you check that the deployed bot works end to end, that it rejects bad input, and that it degrades safely when a dependency fails. At the end you compare your results with the numbers the team measured.
All commands assume stage dev, Region ap-southeast-1, and a shell at the repository root. Lambda function names follow the pattern askfirst-<stage>-<function>.
STAGE=dev export AWS_REGION=ap-southeast-1 5.6.1 Happy path: send a message from Telegram Open your test bot in Telegram, send /start and accept the privacy policy. Send a short made-up suspicious text, for example a message that claims to be from a bank and asks for an OTP. Never use real messages from real people. Expected behaviour: The bot replies with a “⏳” message almost immediately (the webhook function accepted the update and put an AnalyzeJob on SQS). A few seconds later the “⏳” message is edited into the verdict with a risk level and a short explanation (the worker called the ai function and rendered the reply). Send a screenshot of a made-up scam message (an image) and repeat. Images take longer because of OCR (see 5.6.5). 5.6.2 Test the webhook directly with curl The webhook is a public Lambda Function URL (AuthType: NONE). The only authentication is the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header, so the function must reject any request without the right secret. Get the URL from the SAM output WebhookFunctionUrl and read the secret from SSM into a shell variable (do not print it or paste it anywhere):
FUNCTION_URL="<WebhookFunctionUrl from the SAM outputs>" SECRET=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/telegram/webhook_secret" \ --with-decryption --query Parameter.Value --output text) Test Command Expected No secret curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$FUNCTION_URL" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}' UNAUTHORIZED, 401 Wrong secret same, plus -H "X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: wrong" UNAUTHORIZED, 401 Right secret, empty update same, plus -H "X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: $SECRET" IGNORED, 200 Right secret, malformed JSON curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$FUNCTION_URL" -H "X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: $SECRET" -d 'not-json' INVALID_JSON, 400 The expected codes come from WebhookHandler.handleRequest in backend/ScamProtection/webhook-handler. The repository also ships a script that runs the secret checks plus the DynamoDB, S3, SQS and SSM checks in one go:
./infra/verify-dev.sh # Windows: .\infra\verify-dev.ps1 Other edge cases the webhook handles (each returns 200 so Telegram does not retry): the same update_id delivered twice (DUPLICATE), unsupported media such as documents or audio (UNSUPPORTED_*), a user who has not accepted the policy (CONSENT_REQUIRED), and a user over the rate limit (RATE_LIMITED). Test these from the Telegram app rather than with hand-made JSON, because a fake update with a real chat ID makes the bot send real messages.
Actual output on the dev environment (25/11/2026) for the two cases that need no secret:
$ curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$FUNCTION_URL" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}' UNAUTHORIZED 401 $ curl -s -w "\n%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$FUNCTION_URL" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: wrong" -d '{}' UNAUTHORIZED 401 5.6.3 Check the result in CloudWatch Logs and DynamoDB Logs. Each function writes to /aws/lambda/askfirst-<stage>-<function>. Follow the worker while you send a message:
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/askfirst-$STAGE-worker --since 10m --follow Look for a line like ai_invoke op=analyze trace=<id> ms=<ms> outcome=<outcome>. The ai function logs one JSON line per call with the same trace_id, so you can follow one job across both functions:
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/askfirst-$STAGE-ai --since 10m --filter-pattern '"analyze"' Logs contain IDs, operation names, timings, risk level and processing path only. They never contain the message text, the image, or the Telegram file URL (checked over 30 days of logs, docs/results/lambda-p95.md, section Log).
DynamoDB. The worker stores one item per check in the single table askfirst-<stage>, with PK = USER#tg:<telegram_user_id> and SK = CHECK#<check_id>. The item holds the outcome, not the message: level, score, grp, scenario, path, signal_codes, created_at, ttl. On a small dev table a scan is fine:
aws dynamodb scan --table-name askfirst-$STAGE \ --filter-expression "begins_with(SK, :sk)" \ --expression-attribute-values '{":sk":{"S":"CHECK#"}}' \ --expression-attribute-names '{"#l":"level","#p":"path","#s":"score"}' \ --projection-expression "SK, #l, #s, #p, created_at" --max-items 5 path tells you how the verdict was produced: fast (rules were enough), cache, llm (Qwen3 32B judge), escalated (backup model gpt-oss-120b also called) or rules_only (no LLM, see 5.6.4).
5.6.4 Failure scenarios 1. The LLM is down or slow: rules-only fallback. The judge never raises on an LLM error. It returns no judgement and the fuse step scores the message with rules only (ai/src/askfirst/pipeline/judge.py). If the primary model fails, the backup model is tried while time remains. If Bedrock Guardrails cannot be called, the pipeline skips the guard and continues (fail-open). The reply is still sent; the stored path is rules_only.
2. Kill switch. Operators can switch the LLM off without a deploy. The worker reads the item PK = CONFIG#global, SK = FLAGS and caches it for 30 seconds. Check the current value first, because the team’s dev table has had it set to false:
aws dynamodb get-item --table-name askfirst-$STAGE \ --key '{"PK":{"S":"CONFIG#global"},"SK":{"S":"FLAGS"}}' # Turn the LLM off (rules only, the bot shows a maintenance note) aws dynamodb update-item --table-name askfirst-$STAGE \ --key '{"PK":{"S":"CONFIG#global"},"SK":{"S":"FLAGS"}}' \ --update-expression "SET llm_enabled = :v" \ --expression-attribute-values '{":v":{"BOOL":false}}' Wait about 30 seconds, send a message, and check that path is rules_only. Set the value back to true (or to what it was before) when you are done. Other flags in the same item: feature_image, feature_voice, feature_rag.
3. Job fails repeatedly: DLQ. The jobs queue redrives a message to jobs-dlq after 5 failed receives. The worker-dlq function then edits the “⏳” message into a “busy, please try again” message and the alarm askfirst-<stage>-jobs-dlq-not-empty fires (see 5.7). The procedure in infra/WORKER.md forces the failure by throttling the ai function:
QUEUE_URL=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/sqs/jobs_queue_url" --query Parameter.Value --output text) DLQ_URL=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/sqs/jobs_dlq_url" --query Parameter.Value --output text) aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url "$QUEUE_URL" --attributes VisibilityTimeout=20 # speed up retries aws lambda put-function-concurrency --function-name askfirst-$STAGE-ai --reserved-concurrent-executions 0 # send one text message to the bot, wait 2-3 minutes aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$DLQ_URL" --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessages Clean up afterwards:
aws lambda delete-function-concurrency --function-name askfirst-$STAGE-ai aws sqs purge-queue --queue-url "$DLQ_URL" sam deploy ... # puts VisibilityTimeout back to 720 Do not leave the ai function at reserved concurrency 0 or the visibility timeout at 20 seconds. Both break normal traffic.
5.6.5 Measured results The team measured accuracy offline on a labelled dataset and latency on the deployed Lambda functions.
Accuracy (docs/eval-report-final.md, 24/11/2026, prompt judge_v3, 3 independent runs, 134 labelled samples):
Metric Result Target Recall on scam messages (n = 90) 100% in all 3 runs ≥ 90% False alarm on benign but suspicious-looking messages (n = 20) 5% in all 3 runs ≤ 10% False alarm on normal benign messages 0% Correct risk level 99.3% LLM token cost per check 0.000792 USD The dataset was written or rewritten by the team; it has 0 real anonymized samples, and 1 sample equals 5 percentage points of false alarm. Treat these numbers as an upper bound. To reproduce (needs Bedrock access, run from ai/):
AWS_PROFILE=<your-bedrock-profile> uv run --with "botocore[crt]" python ../eval/run_eval.py \ ../eval/datasets/{benign_normal,benign_suspicious,hard,real_scam}.ai1.jsonl ../eval/datasets/hard.jsonl \ --pipeline real --out ../eval/out/run1 --cache ../eval/out/run1/cache Latency on Lambda (docs/results/lambda-p95.md, ai at 3008 MB, ap-southeast-1):

title: Monitoring
content:
This page shows the monitoring that the stack actually has today and how to look at it. It is deliberately small: CloudWatch Logs, the built-in Lambda and SQS metrics, one alarm on the DLQ, an optional SNS email for that alarm, and AWS Budgets on the account.
What Exists in the stack? Where it is defined Lambda log groups (webhook, worker, worker-dlq, ai) Yes, created by Lambda on first run automatic Log retention No, logs are kept forever not set in infra/template.yaml Built-in metrics (AWS/Lambda, AWS/SQS, AWS/DynamoDB) Yes automatic Custom metrics No the code does not publish any yet Alarm askfirst-<stage>-jobs-dlq-not-empty Yes JobsDlqAlarm in infra/template.yaml SNS email for the alarm Optional parameter AlarmTopicArn; the topic is not created by the stack CloudWatch dashboard No AWS Budgets (10, 25, 50 USD) Yes, on the account created by hand (task BE-01), see infra/README.md 5.7.1 CloudWatch Logs Each function writes to /aws/lambda/askfirst-<stage>-<function>. Useful log lines:
Function Line Meaning worker ai_invoke op=<op> trace=<id> ms=<ms> outcome=<outcome> one call from the worker to ai worker job_failed type=<job> job=<id> ... error=<code> a job failed; SQS will retry it ai JSON line with trace_id, op, ms, result one call handled by ai all REPORT ... Duration ... Init Duration written by Lambda; Init Duration appears only on a cold start Tail a log group from the CLI:
aws logs tail /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-worker --since 1h --follow In the console: CloudWatch → Logs → Log groups → /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-worker → Search log group.
5.7.2 CloudWatch Logs Insights queries Open CloudWatch → Logs → Logs Insights, choose the log groups, set the time range, and paste a query. These are the queries the team used for docs/results/lambda-p95.md and the blog draft on the INIT limit.
Cold starts (run on /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-ai and /aws/lambda/askfirst-dev-worker):
filter @type = "REPORT" and ispresent(@initDuration) | stats count() as cold_starts, pct(@initDuration, 50) as p50, pct(@initDuration, 95) as p95, max(@initDuration) as max_ms INIT phases that hit the 10-second limit (see 5.10):
filter @message like /INIT_REPORT/ and @message like /timeout/ | fields @timestamp, @message | sort @timestamp desc Failed jobs in the worker:
filter @message like /job_failed/ | fields @timestamp, @message | sort @timestamp desc | limit 50 Calls from the worker to ai:
filter @message like /ai_invoke/ | fields @timestamp, @message | sort @timestamp desc | limit 50 5.7.3 Built-in metrics Lambda and SQS publish metrics without any code. In CloudWatch → Metrics → All metrics:
Lambda → By Function Name: Invocations, Errors, Duration, Throttles, ConcurrentExecutions for each askfirst-dev-* function. SQS → Queue Metrics: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage for askfirst-dev-jobs and askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq. The Lambda console also shows these under Lambda → Functions → askfirst-dev-worker → Monitor.
5.7.4 The DLQ alarm The only alarm in the template is askfirst-<stage>-jobs-dlq-not-empty. It uses metric math MAX([visible, received]) on the DLQ (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible and NumberOfMessagesReceived, period 60 s) and goes to ALARM when the value is ≥ 1, meaning at least one job failed 5 times. Missing data counts as OK. SQS metrics arrive a few minutes late.
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty \ --query "MetricAlarms[0].[AlarmName,StateValue,StateReason]" --output table To see it fire, use the DLQ test in 5.6.4.
5.7.5 Optional: email notification through SNS Without AlarmTopicArn the alarm still changes state but notifies nobody. The stack does not create the topic, so create it yourself and pass its ARN at deploy time:
TOPIC_ARN=$(aws sns create-topic --name askfirst-dev-alarms --query TopicArn --output text) aws sns subscribe --topic-arn "$TOPIC_ARN" --protocol email --notification-endpoint <your-email> # confirm the subscription from the email AWS sends you, then: sam deploy --parameter-overrides Stage=dev AlarmTopicArn="$TOPIC_ARN" ... # keep your other overrides The team’s dev stack attached the topic askfirst-dev-alarms on 25/11/2026 (only the AlarmTopicArn parameter changed; the change set modified only JobsDlqAlarm). To test the email without breaking a job, force the alarm into ALARM; it returns to OK at the next evaluation:
aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --alarm-name askfirst-dev-jobs-dlq-not-empty \ --state-value ALARM --state-reason "Test SNS email" Test on 25/11/2026: the alarm history shows Successfully executed action on the topic, SNS NumberOfNotificationsDelivered = 2 (the ALARM email and the OK email), NumberOfNotificationsFailed = 0.
5.7.6 Gaps you should know about No log retention. Log groups never expire. The cost estimate recommends RetentionInDays: 7 for the three functions (docs/results/cost-estimate.md, section 5). No custom metrics, no dashboard, one alarm. The cost estimate budgets for 5 custom metrics, 5 alarms and 1 dashboard, but these are planned work, not deployed. No alarm on the kill switch or on cost. Cost is watched only through AWS Budgets on the account.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Overall impressions of the program First Cloud AI Journey let me build a real project end to end on AWS instead of isolated labs: proposal, serverless architecture, Bedrock, CI/CD, cost measurement and clean-up. Working as a team with issues, PR reviews and ADRs got me used to how a software team operates. The program’s rules site states the requirements and the scoring clearly, so it is easy to check my own work against it.
Satisfaction 4.5/5. I learned the most from getting an AI model running on AWS and measuring it with real numbers. Half a point off because some requirements changed close to the deadline.
What could be improved The rules were updated on 21–24/11 (the Step-by-step Lab Guide became mandatory) while the deadline is 30/11, leaving teams little time to adjust. Fixing requirements earlier, or announcing changes with a transition period, would help. Getting Bedrock model access and a team AWS account took time early on; a guide or ready accounts from week one would help AI teams avoid delays. A sample workshop for a multi-service project (not only a single-service lab) would show interns how much detail is expected. Would I recommend it to friends? Why? Yes. It suits anyone who wants to learn cloud and AI by building a real project, with a team workflow and access to AWS services that are hard to try on your own. I would tell them to plan for a significant time commitment.

title: Clean Up
content:
When you finish the workshop, delete everything in the order below so nothing keeps billing. Steps 1–6 follow the clean-up guide in the project repository (infra/README.md, section 7, rewritten in pull request #186 for task SH-10). Step 7 and the extra items in steps 5 and 6 cover resources created in other sections of this workshop.
The commands are for stage dev in ap-southeast-1, run from the repository root in Bash (on Windows use Git Bash or WSL). Change STAGE if you deployed another stage.
STAGE=dev export AWS_REGION=ap-southeast-1 Steps 3, 5 and 6 cannot be undone. Step 3 deletes every file in the bucket (models and donated images). Step 5 deletes the DynamoDB table askfirst-$STAGE with all user data, and its PITR backups go with it. Step 6 deletes the bot token parameter and all logs. Back up anything you want to keep first.
Step 1: Remove the Telegram webhook Stop Telegram from sending updates to the Function URL before the function is deleted:
python scripts/set_webhook.py --delete # reads TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN from the environment or .env Check: the script prints a successful deleteWebhook result, and the bot’s getWebhookInfo shows an empty url.
Step 2: Remove provisioned concurrency (only if you turned it on) The template does not enable provisioned concurrency. If you added it yourself, remove it:
for f in webhook worker ai; do aws lambda list-provisioned-concurrency-configs --function-name askfirst-$STAGE-$f \ --query 'ProvisionedConcurrencyConfigs[].FunctionArn' --output text 2>/dev/null done # For every line printed, delete the config on that alias, for example: aws lambda delete-provisioned-concurrency-config --function-name askfirst-$STAGE-ai --qualifier live Check: running the loop again prints nothing.
Step 3: Empty the S3 bucket CloudFormation cannot delete a bucket that still has objects. The stack’s bucket does not have versioning, but if you turned it on you must also delete old versions:
BUCKET=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name "/askfirst/$STAGE/s3/bucket_name" --query Parameter.Value --output text) aws s3 rm "s3://$BUCKET" --recursive # Only if versioning was enabled: delete every version and delete marker aws s3api delete-objects --bucket "$BUCKET" --delete "$(aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket "$BUCKET" \ --query '{Objects: [Versions, DeleteMarkers][][].{Key: Key, VersionId: VersionId}}' --output json)" Check: aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket "$BUCKET" --max-items 1 shows no Versions or DeleteMarkers. The bucket itself is deleted in step 5.
Step 4: Delete the ECR images The repository askfirst-ai belongs to the stack askfirst-github-oidc and has EmptyOnDelete: true, so deleting the stack deletes the images too:
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name askfirst-github-oidc aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --stack-name askfirst-github-oidc Check: aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names askfirst-ai returns RepositoryNotFoundException. If another stack in the account shares the GitHub OIDC provider, review this stack before deleting it.
Step 5: Delete the SAM stack If you gave the ai function access to Bedrock in another account (infra/README.md, section 8.4), remove the inline policy you added by hand to its role first. CloudFormation did not create that policy:
aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name <AI_LAMBDA_ROLE> --policy-name assume-bedrock Then delete the stack:
sam delete --stack-name askfirst-$STAGE Answer y when SAM asks to delete the stack and its artifacts.
